issues.legal_issue: Long and quiet possession does not support a presumption of a lost grant in favour of possessors when convincing evidence establishes the nature of the grant and identifies its grantee.
material_facts: The original grant document was unavailable, and the archakas and their predecessors had possessed the properties for a long time.
The Inam Register and the archakas’ predecessors’ statement from the Inam inquiry identified the temple as the grantee and did not identify the archakas as grantees or holders of an interest.
issues.conclusion: The evidence identifying the temple as grantee precluded a presumption of a lost grant in favour of the archakas; the deity was the grantee.
issues.legal_principle: A presumption of lawful title based on long and quiet possession may support possessory rights when actual proof of title is absent, but it cannot be made where sufficient and convincing evidence establishes the grant’s nature and grantee. The Court referred generally to judicial decisions supporting the lost-grant presumption but named no such decisions. The Inam inquiry and register were considered in the context of the temple’s notification under Chapter VIA of the Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1927.

predicates.temple_property_possession_suit: A suit is brought to recover possession of property claimed for a temple.
predicates.long_quiet_possession: The possessors or their predecessors have held the property for a long time and quietly.
predicates.convincing_grant_evidence_identifies_ano: Reliable evidence establishes the grant’s nature and identifies someone other than the possessors as its grantee.

issues.definition: When a temple-property possession suit involves long and quiet possession but convincing evidence identifies another grantee, the rule denies the possessors a lost-grant presumption.

issues.legal_issue: Equality between the assessment recorded for an inam and the income recorded for it does not, by itself, establish that the grant comprised only melvaram rights.
material_facts: The appellants argued that the grant was limited to melvaram rights, relying on a decision involving equal assessment and income figures.
In this case, the assessment figure in the Inam Register and the income figure in the Inam Statement were different.
The Court explained that the register recorded assessment in the same form whether the grant comprised both land interests or only melvaram rights.
issues.conclusion: The Court rejected the inference that equal assessment and income figures, by themselves, show a grant limited to melvaram rights.
issues.legal_principle: The entries in an Inam Register must be interpreted in light of the form used for recording grants: an assessment entry is required whether the grant comprises the land itself or only melvaram rights. The Court rejected the reasoning in the unreported Madras High Court decision in Appeal No. 213 of 1942, Board of Commissioners for the Hindu Religious Endowments, Madras v. Parasaram Veeraraghavacharyulu and others, and noted that it had been dissented from in Yelamanchili Venkatadri v. Vedantam Seshacharyulu and others.

predicates.inam_grant_scope_dispute: The parties dispute whether an inam grant comprised the land itself or only the revenue interest.
predicates.assessment_and_income_figures_match: The amount recorded as the assessment and the amount recorded as income from the inam are equal.

issues.definition: In a dispute about the scope of an inam grant, matching assessment and income figures alone do not establish that the grant was limited to melvaram rights.

issues.legal_issue: A grant to a temple comprises both interests in the land when the grant records identify the temple as grantee and the evidence does not establish that the archakas held the underlying land interest before the grant.
material_facts: The Inam Register classified the grant as a Devadayam, described it as being for the support of a temple, and named the temple as the original grantee.
The archakas’ statement from the Inam inquiry also named the temple, not the archakas, as the inamdar and present enjoyer.
The evidence did not establish that the archakas had kudivaram rights before the grant.
The assessment and income figures in the two records differed.
issues.conclusion: The grant in favour of the temple comprised both melvaram and kudivaram interests, that is, the land itself.
issues.legal_principle: The Court determined the scope of the grant from the documentary entries and the evidence concerning prior rights. It rejected the view that the assessment entry alone limited a grant to melvaram rights, distinguishing Board of Commissioners for the Hindu Religious Endowments, Madras v. Parasaram Veeraraghavacharyulu and others and preferring the approach in Yelamanchili Venkatadri v. Vedantam Seshacharyulu and others.

predicates.inam_grant_scope_dispute: The parties dispute whether an inam grant comprised the land itself or only the revenue interest.
predicates.grant_records_identify_temple_as_grantee: The records of the grant identify the temple as the grantee.
predicates.no_evidence_of_archakas_prior_land_right: The evidence does not establish that the archakas held the underlying land interest before the grant.

issues.definition: Where the grant records identify the temple as grantee and no evidence establishes prior land rights in the archakas, the grant includes both land interests.

issues.legal_issue: Moral or equitable claims of temple servants do not justify allowing them to retain temple property in an ejectment suit based on proven title when they assert an adverse title against the temple.
material_facts: The suit sought ejectment of archakas and persons claiming through them after the temple’s executive officer demanded possession.
The Court found that the temple had title under the grant.
The archakas claimed the properties as their own, contrary to their predecessors’ statement identifying the temple as grantee.
The facts needed to assess the income, service expenses, reasonable remuneration, and past appropriations had not been investigated.
issues.conclusion: The archakas were not entitled to equitable relief allowing them to remain in possession; their moral claims were out of place in this ejectment suit, particularly given their adverse claim against the temple.
issues.legal_principle: Claims, even moral rather than legal ones, of archakas may be considered in a proceeding to frame a scheme for a temple, but those considerations are out of place in an ejectment suit brought on proof of title, especially when the archakas assert an adverse title and deny the temple’s title. The Court referred to Dandibhotla Kutumba Sastrulu v. Kontharapu Venkatalingam and an unreported Madras High Court decision in Appeal No. 709 of 1944, but held that scheme-related considerations did not warrant relief in this ejectment suit.

predicates.ejectment_suit_on_proven_temple_title: A suit seeks to eject occupants from property after the temple’s title to it has been established.
predicates.claimants_are_temple_archakas: The occupants seeking to retain possession are archakas serving the temple.
predicates.claimants_assert_adverse_title_against_t: The archakas claim the property as their own and deny the temple’s title.

issues.definition: When archakas contest a temple’s established title in an ejectment suit by asserting ownership themselves, their moral or equitable claim does not entitle them to retain possession.
